utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Judge Thelin is unable to be here today. We have decided in the circumstances it will be appropriate to continue sitting without him, and I hope my voice lasts the day or else we'd be down to one Judge. Now, where had we got to? Are you finished, Mr. Shin?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, I think we were in cross-examination by Mr. Powles.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: I think we were part way through cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Mr. Bouckaert, you will be pleased to hear there's not much left for you on Mr. Musliu's behalf. You gave two statements to the Office of the Prosecutor. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: One was in March of 1999, and the second on the 20th of April, 2004?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: And presumably you were given an opportunity to go over those statements before you gave evidence on Friday in court?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Now, on Friday, you accepted that one of the aims of the KLA was to protect the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we differed a bit on that point. That was one of the aims but not the principal aim.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Not the principal but you accept it was one of. One of the aims of the Kosovo Liberation Army was to protect the civilian population. And you may recall that I asked you for some examples of the Kosovo Liberation Army so protecting the civilian population and you were unable to think of any on the spot.

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: I wonder, over the weekend, whether you'd been able to think of any more.

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't review it, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: No. Do you have a copy of your March 1999 statement with you, Mr. Bouckaert?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no documents with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: I wonder if Mr. Younis would be helpful enough to provide -- perhaps I should have flagged it up with Mr. Younis beforehand.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: We don't actually have that document at hand at this moment. If counsel has a copy that the witness could have before him, that would be very helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: What I may do is read you a portion of your statement.

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: And see if you accept that now.

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: I suspect you will. In your March 1999 statement, at page 20, you say the following, and I'll read it as slowly as I can for the purposes of interpretation. You said: "At Kishna Reka the conditions were rapidly deteriorating." And you refer to some photographs. You say: "There was limited clean water available and many people had begun suffering from respiratory illnesses and illnesses associated with crowded living conditions. A plastic-covered shelter -- shelters were providing insufficient -- proving insufficient to protect the displaced persons from the elements and the IDPs --" that's presumably internally displaced persons?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: "... the IDPs remained fearful of an attack by Yugoslav forces." And you say this: "Similar attacks on displaced persons had taken place at Senik, Sedlare, and Vranic among other places. There appeared to be a slight UCK presence behind the camp but Human Rights Watch did not see any presence within the camp. I raised our concerns at the checkpoint with the UCK, urging them that the refugees would remain clearly separate from any UCK presence. The UCK's response was that Yugoslav authorities had not shown any distinction between civilian and military targets through their offensive but they had taken precaution to keep their small military presence separate from the refugee camp. It appeared that they wanted to keep a small presence reasonably close to the camp to afford some protection to the displaced persons." Do you, first of all, accept that that is what you said in your March 1999 statement?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: So you would accept from that that, first of all, the IDPs had a fear of attack from Yugoslav forces?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: And that there was a KLA presence behind but not in the camp?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was very close to the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Yes. And the KLA's reasons for wanting to be --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. We do have a copy of the statement. If we could have that placed before the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And I'm very grateful to Mr. Younis who appears to have done a 200-yard dash or so to get these.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: I'm even more grateful to Mr. Younis. Thank you very much, Mr. Younis.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Mr. Bouckaert, it's at page 20 and 21.

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Yes. So the final thing you say in your statement, I think on page 21, is that the KLA's intention in keeping a small presence close to the camp was to it be able to afford some protection to the civilians based there.

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That appeared to be -- that was the stated intent of the UCK to us. However, we were concerned that their close presence to this IDP camp also endangered the IDPs themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the reason why I approached the checkpoint is because we were concerned about shielding, but I would agree with you that it was the stated intent of the UCK to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That they were there to protect the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Exactly. You may have had your concerns, Mr. Bouckaert --

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: -- but the reality is that the stated aim given to you, and it seems an aim that you accept in your statement in that you say this, and I shall quote you on page 21, it's the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: "It appeared --" indicating perhaps that you accepted what they said to you -- "It appeared that they wanted to keep a small presence reasonably close to the camp to afford some protection to the displaced persons." So you accept that it appeared to be their genuine aim to try and keep some presence there in order to afford a protection to the civilians so placed there.

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was their stated aim to us, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: And that's what you say in your statement.

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my statement, I say that it appeared that they wanted to keep a small presence reasonably close to the camp to afford some protection to the displaced persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: But we disagreed with the wisdom of that practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: All right. Moving on, then, to the structure of the Kosovo Liberation Army. Just clarify the dates that you're actually in Kosovo. It's three weeks in September 1998, three weeks in November of 1998.

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: In 1998 that was the sum total of the time that you spent in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the sum total I spent in Kosovo in 1998, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: So any assistance you give in relation outside of those dates is based on information that you were given by other people?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Yes. It's right, isn't it, that after the Drenica massacres in February and March of 1998 the KLA grew at a massive rate?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: And all manner of people joined the KLA; farmers, returned asylum seekers, so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I even ran into some people from New York City.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Right. So it's fair to say that many people, if not the majority of people who joined the KLA at that time, did not have much military experience.

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their military experience varied tremendously. There was a -- some people that we met who had prior experience in the Yugoslav army, especially at the command level, but there were many people who were simple farmers or pizza boys from New York, people like that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Yes. It's right to say that those who had certainly officer experience with the JNA, that a fair number of them, instead of joining the KLA in fact joined an organisation knows as the F-A-R-K, the FARK. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that would overstate the importance of the FARK. There were -- there were a number of former JNA officers who joined the FARK, but it remained a relatively marginal organisation in the overall military situation in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Have you got the bundle of exhibits with you, Mr. Bouckaert?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: If they could be given to you, if not.

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, I don't. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: If could you turn to tab 5, pages 92 and 93.

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And just for the record, that's Prosecution Exhibit 212.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Page 92 and 93 -- are you there, Mr. Bouckaert?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: At the bottom of page 92, the last paragraph, you refer to the July 1998 offensive by the Yugoslav forces and you say as a result of that that it appeared that the command structure had been damaged as a result of that offensive. I should say, rather than you say that, that's what the report --

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: -- says. And then you say -- the report says the following: "Complicating the matter is the recent rise of a separate armed Albanian organisation known as FARK ... which has a separate base in Northern Albania and is mostly present in the Metohija ... region of Kosovo. By September 1998, it was clear that this alternative group, comprised mostly of ethnic Albanians with past experience in the Yugoslav army and police --" and then over the page it says this, it "did not agree with the UCK's military strategy, criticising its lack of professionalism. FARK, however, apparently did not exist as an organised force until August 1998." From that, is it fair to extrapolate that those with experience from the Yugoslav forces, a lot of them did actually join the FARK?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again I would differ with your use of the word "a lot of them." What we say in the report is that most of the people who joined the FARK --

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- either had police or military experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: But that does not mean that the majority of people with military or police experience --

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Yes, I --

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- joined the FARK. And many of the officers, KLA officers that we met similarly had prior military or police experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Right. Certainly, though, it was the view of at least some of those within FARK that they did not agree with the UCK's military strategy and were -- they were critical of its lack of professionalism.

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: When Mr. Younis gave you a copy of this statement, your statement, did he give you a copy of your April 2004 statement as well?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: It's right, isn't it, that when you met with Mr. Limaj and Mr. Thaqi, it's right, isn't it, that one of the things that Mr. Thaqi explained to you when you met him in November of 1998, one of the things that he told you was that the KLA was a new army and was only just formalising its structures. Do you remember him telling you that?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said, if I remember correctly, that -- his comments about KLA's new structures related to the civilian structures being created in Drenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: If you could turn to page 7 of your 2004 statement, specifically at paragraph 36.

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: You say the following: "It is difficult for me to remember the precise conversation conducted during the meeting. We talked about the structure of the KLA and its obligations under the Geneva Conventions, and then you say this: "At this stage Thaqi explained that the UCK was a new army and only just formalising its structures."

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. So I would --

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Thank you. Returning then to the bundle of exhibits, tab 5 again, Humanitarian Law Violations in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: It's just a couple of dates in relation to the matters that occurred at Orahovac. If you could turn to page 4 of that document please, Mr. Bouckaert.

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: It's the third paragraph.

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Is it correct that the report says the following: "The UCK's first major offensive began on July 19 when it attempted to capture the town of Orahovac. The attempt failed as the police recaptured the town two days later."

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: So that would put the date of the KLA's offensive as the 19th and then two days later when the Serbs retook it being the 21st of July?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: And it's right, isn't it, that the Serb or the Yugoslav forces had very little trouble retaking territory from the KLA as part of that July offensive?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they certainly destroyed a lot of Orahovac, including several of the mosques in their counter-offensive, but it was not a very extensive battle, I would agree with that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: And generally -- leaving Orahovac to one side, generally in relation to the July offensive, the Serbs had little trouble retaking territory from the KLA.

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the KLA, as most guerrilla armies, did not focus much of its military potential on trying to hold onto territory. Whenever the Yugoslav forces went into even Drenica, the KLA would quickly disappear or retreat from most of its positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: And then come back after the Yugoslav forces withdrew. That was the pattern that we generally observed.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Yes. Moving on, then, to the -- to the context of what was going on in 1998, and in particular the activities of Yugoslav forces and authorities, you said, I think, on Friday that during the period of the conflict, presumably 1998, the vast majority of people abused were those abused by the Yugoslav forces.

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yugoslav and Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Yugoslav and Serbian forces. And I think, again turning to tab 5, the Humanitarian Law Violations in Kosovo report by Human Rights Watch, I believe at page 3 in the summary in the first paragraph it's stated: "The vast majority of these abuses were committed by government forces of the Serbian special police (MUP) or the Yugoslav army."

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: A little later on down the page it says that the UCK or KLA has also committed -- "has also violated the laws of war ... Although on a lesser scale than the government abuses, these too are violations of international standards ..." So it was certainly the view of the Human Rights Watch that the vast majority of abuses were being committed by Serb forces at that time and the most serious abuses were being committed by the Serb forces as well.

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The vast majority of abuses, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Right. In the Human Rights Watch report A Week of Terror in Drenica - I think that's at tab 3, if I'm not mistaken, of your bundle - is that the complete report there or just a small portion of it?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. It's a report which is as long as the Humanitarian Law Violations in Kosovo report.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: So have you got the complete report or just --

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I only have the short section which the OTP copied.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: I know that copies were -- well, actually, the page I intend to refer to is here, so if I may hand it up.

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Could I just have the reference to what that page number is.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Yes. It's page 16, Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: The third page in that small bundle.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: The first paragraph the following is stated: "In mid-July 1998, the Yugoslav army and Serbian police began a major offensive against the KLA, which had assumed loose control of an estimated one-third of Kosovo. The offensive, which involved heavy artillery, tanks, and occasional airpower, was highly effective in driving the KLA from most of its Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. established positions into pockets in the mountains and woods." The crucial part is the following paragraph: "In the end, however, very few KLA fighters were killed or captured. The brunt of suffering was borne by ethnic Albanian civilians who lived in the areas of conflict. More than 200 villages were destroyed..." Is that a figure that you would accept, Mr. Bouckaert?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the figure that I wrote, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: " ... at least 300.000 people were internally displaced." Again, presumably a figure you accept?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: And: "Most of the estimated 2.000 people killed through September were civilians." It's one of the aims of Human Rights Watch, or one of the desires of Human Rights Watch to ensure accountability, to ensure that those who commit attacks on the civilian population are brought to justice.

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: And certainly the view of Human Rights Watch that tolerating human rights abuse would be catastrophic.

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Now, given that the majority of crimes in 1998 were committed by Serb forces, are you aware of any members of Serb or Yugoslav forces being prosecuted for their crimes in 1998?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: No. Do either you or indeed Human Rights Watch have any concern that this Tribunal has not sought to bring to justice any of the offenders responsible for crimes in 1998?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the person most responsible for those abuses is Slobodan Milosevic --

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- who is on trial in front of this Tribunal. And some of the evidence included in this report, including the massacre at Gornje Obrinje, has been brought before this Court --

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- in that Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Yes. But you're aware that he's not charged with any crimes or offences in 1998?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: And you're also aware that nobody has specifically been prosecuted for violations on the Serb side for any offences committed within 1998?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: We will continue to fully cooperate with this Tribunal to bring to justice any of the perpetrators of crimes against humanity or war crimes committed during this period.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: And again I put the question to you Mr. Bouckaert: Do either you or Human Rights Watch have any concern that none of the offenders responsible for crimes in 1998 have not been prosecuted by this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: We certainly would like to see the perpetrators of those crimes prosecuted by this Tribunal, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Yes. Moving on to just a couple of other small matters: You said on Friday that Mr. Demaci of the KLA gave you a special pass to travel in KLA areas in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: So although he may have been, according to you, asleep at some times during the day, thereby unable to give you a pass, in principle it was something that the KLA were prepared to grant to you.

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And as I think I said, we had very good cooperation with the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: They also treated us -- always treated us quite professionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Yes. By contrast, the MUP and Yugoslav military authorities placed severe travel restrictions on you, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We couldn't even get visas from the Serbian authorities. We had to go to Montenegro to get our visas extended and we often did not get travel permission from them or any cooperation and often found ourselves in very threatening situations with the Yugoslav authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: And it's fair to say that, as well as making things difficult for you, they also made it difficult if not impossible for investigators from the ICTY to move freely and investigate allegations within Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they refused to acknowledge the jurisdiction of the OTP and this Tribunal over the events in Kosovo and repeatedly barred the Prosecutor's office from entering Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Now, I think on Friday when dealing with the release of the two Tanjug journalists, which had occurred after your meeting with Mr. Limaj and Mr. Thaqi, I think you thanked Mr. Limaj for the fact that they were released shortly after the meeting you had with him and Mr. Thaqi.

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: It's right, though, that in neither of your statements, both the 1999 statement nor the 2004 statement, is it implied that either Mr. Limaj or Mr. Thaqi had any say or control over whether those two journalists would be released.

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: In fact, it's the opposite that's stated in your statement, certainly the March 1999 statement. It's said that Mr. Thaqi and Mr. Limaj conveyed to both you and Mr. Abrams that, as military commanders, they could not interfere in the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, if you're going to refer to a specific reference to the witness's statement, if the witness could please have that put in front of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Sure. It's page 18 of the March 1999 statement, Mr. Bouckaert.

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: In thanking Mr. Limaj I did not mean to imply that he played a direct role in the release.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: In fact the point is this: You were told specifically at that meeting that it was, as military commanders, not a matter in which they could interfere.

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: They said they could not interfere in the judicial proceedings, so we alternatively asked them as the military authorities to grant -- to grant the two journalists amnesty.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: That's not something stated in your statement, is it?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but that's what I stated in testimony before this Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: In relation to any sort of prison or detention facility in Lapusnik, it's right that you never heard of such a prison camp or detention facility in Lapusnik during your time in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. The only prison facilities that I heard about were a facility near Malisevo which was mentioned by a Serb who had escaped from KLA custody and a prison known as prison number 7, which -- the location of which we did not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: No. It's right also, Mr. Bouckaert, that you never met or heard of my client Mr. Isak Musliu?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Either by that name or by his nom de guerre Qerqiz?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Which, of course, is a shortened version of Qerqiz Topoli, a famous Albanian national hero.

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: You also mentioned on Friday that one of the sources from which you got information during your time in Kosovo was from the Council for the Defence of Human Rights and Freedoms.

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Can you confirm that they are a reliable source of information?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had some difficulties with some of their material at times.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: But it's fair to say that they were of assistance to you in providing information to you?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were of assistance to us, but we would not use their information in our reports without confirmation, in the same way that we were willing to give credibility to the information provided to us by the Humanitarian Law Centre in Kosovo. There are cases where we investigated allegations made by the council where their allegations turned out to be inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Right. Similarly, there must have been examples when their allegations turned out to be accurate?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The speakers are kindly requested to slow down and make pauses.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Finally, Mr. Bouckaert --

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly by saying that we had some problems with some of their information I certainly would not wish to suggest that they were not of extreme assistance to us on an almost daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Finally, if you could just turn to your 1999 statement, I think at page 9.

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: You refer, about halfway down the page, referring to photos 353 to 355, you refer to "Photos of Cen --"

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dugolli.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: -- "Dugolli and family. Dugolli died in custody. Subject of October and December 1998 Human Rights Watch reports." Do you remember off the top of your head what the circumstances of his death were?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was -- the case is documented in our report. He was one of the people who was tortured to death in Yugoslav custody.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Bouckaert. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Bouckaert. My name is Richard Harvey, and together with my friend Mr. Guy-Smith we represent Mr. Haradin Bala who sits in the middle behind us, and again I'm sure you have had no contact with and never heard of the name Haradin Bala except, of course, in connection with these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not before today, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Just a very few questions concerning general conditions in Kosovo at a time when you weren't there. So appreciating the difficulties that we both have in that respect, you have to rely on information provided by others, and you have to evaluate how much those sources of information can indeed be trusted.

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And one of those sources was just referred to in a little detail by my friend Mr. Powles, the Council for Defence of Human Rights and Freedoms. Would it be fair to say that during the 1998 period with which we are primarily concerned here, which is up until the end of July of that year, obtaining reliable sources of information on almost anything was extremely difficult?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was easier to obtain information about things which happened close to towns like Pristina or Pec. In the countryside, access problems made it often very difficult to find reliable information on a timely basis. So often what we would have to do ourselves, as well as other human rights organisations, is to wait until after offensive was completed and areas opened up again to go visit and confirm information.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I'm trying to keep an eye on the interpreters so that I'm not speaking over you or over their interpretation of you, so --

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: -- if there's a little bit of a pause between me -- between you finishing an answer and me asking a question, it's not because I'm a terribly slow thinker, I hope. When you were therefore after the event seeking to investigate allegations of war crimes, human rights abuses, it was very important to speak to people like the Council for Defence of Human Rights and Freedoms?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because they were one of the few organisations with a very extensive network of local activists on the ground in almost every village, so they would often get the first reports from the ground about abuses that had occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And when you would meet with them, of course you've used the word "activists" and it's a very important word in this context. Human Rights Watch does not consider itself an organisation of activists; would that be fair to say?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: We consider ourselves first and foremost a research and advocacy organisation, but we do have an activist streak at times.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: But when dealing with activists, you are always conscious of the potential for some degree of bias, and that's why you look for corroboration from other sources; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, and I think it's perfectly understandable that when a community documents abuses committed against their own community it's much more difficult to have a degree of objectivity about what is happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: From the Council for Defence of Human Rights and Freedoms you obtained documentation of abuses in the form of medical reports of people who alleged that they had been tortured or abused in custody by the police?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Or by the Yugoslav army?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And we also assisted them in bringing about a more professional methodology on the part of their staff, explaining to them why it was important to get medical reports and photographic documentation. It's important to understand that the council had already been doing this for nearly a decade and because serious police abuse was -- had been widespread in Kosovo since 1990. So they were quite an experienced organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Thank you. In that work did you meet members of the council who were doctors?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: We met doctors who were associated with the council but who mostly worked for the Mother Teresa Society.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I was going to come to the Mother Teresa Society. That was another useful source and valuable source of information for you?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Do you remember the names of any of the doctors that you worked with?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall their names, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Let me toss one at you and see if it bites. Dr. Selimi, Dr. Fetim Selimi?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do believe that we met Dr. Selimi, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: A thoracic surgeon by area of expertise?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: He was one of the doctors who cooperated with you and assisted you in your work?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: You mentioned -- you mentioned difficulties of access in researching allegations of human rights abuses. I want to ask you a little more about that in connection with another comment that you were asked about on Friday. That's the 40 per cent control comment. As I understood you, you were saying that you looked at a map between you. You looked at the area of Drenica, and you looked at the map in general and you figured, well, that's about 40 per cent that the KLA controls.

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- we certainly did look at the map and at the areas under KLA control at the time. We consulted pretty widely with various sources in Kosovo as this was obviously not just of relevance to us. And it certainly was an estimate based on looking at the map and matching it up with some of the data that we had, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: The word I want to home in on here is "control."

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Clearly there was a time when the Serbs -- when Federal Republic of Yugoslavia controlled all of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: There then became -- came about periods during 1998 in particular when they lost control over certain areas of the former Yugoslavia, of Kosovo and Albania?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: At that point, I think you would accept, there is a big distinction to be made between loss of control on the one hand and acquisition and implementation of control on the other?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: For instance, if we take that period of 1998 up until the end of July, would you agree that control over major roads, the asphalted roads was a frequently fluctuating situation?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Outside some main Serbian checkpoints, some permanent checkpoints, control certainly was very fluid, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: That distribution of food to the population was often very severely disrupted?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the Yugoslav authorities and on a few minor occasions by the KLA, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And that provision of hospital resources and medical supplies was likewise often severely disrupted.

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And we repeatedly had to interrupt our work to evacuate gravely wounded civilians and argue with Yugoslav authorities at the checkpoints to get them to hospital treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Did you encounter the phenomenon then that those who have been involved in other human rights inquiries have come across which is that wounded civilians are very reluctant to go to state hospitals because, of course, the police are often on the lookout for people who may have been wounded in some kind of armed confrontation?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was even worse than that in Kosovo because many of the state hospitals had been purged of Albanian doctors and refused to even treat Albanian civilians. But certainly wounded people, especially young men, were very afraid to go to the hospitals to seek treatment. Young ethnic Albanian men.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Was it also your experience that medical facilities available to people in the areas -- in areas such as Drenica were pretty ad hoc in the sense that you had a doctor who would be available in one particular town or -- for a while and would have some supplies, and they would have as much difficulty really funneling medical supplies in on the medical side as, say, the military people might have funneling weapons in on the military side?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Drenica particularly you're talking about a very rural area, mostly consisting of villages. Other parts of Kosovo are a little more developed and have at least some mid-sized towns where people have access to a broader range of medical assistance and pharmacies, but particularly in Drenica there was very limited health care available. There were some courageous ethnic Albanian doctors who had actually moved into Drenica to provide medical assistance to people under very difficult conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Certainly for anybody with a severe heart condition, living in that kind of area would have grave difficulty getting access to, really, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. good medical treatment?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: The figure of internally displaced persons, IDPs as they're shortened to be, 300.000 was thrown out just now. I've heard estimates as high as over a million. Would you be in a position to comment on those figures?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: We used the figure 300.000 because that was the figure used at the time of the publication of the report by UNHCR and other UN agencies, but obviously it was a very fluid situation. People were sometimes displaced just for days and significant populations, because of the widespread destruction of civilian infrastructure, entire villages being burned by the Serbs, by the Yugoslav forces, were displaced much longer term. There were also people who fled to -- to Montenegro and to Albania. There is a more detailed breakdown of the figure in the week of Drenica -- Week of Terror in Drenica report, which was not included in the section excerpt.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And just finally on this question of control, you've already been asked about the KLA during that period up until the end of July. Clearly the Yugoslav authorities would never deign to refer to the KLA as an army. That much is well established, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They would refer to them as terrorists in the ordinary course of conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: On the other side, the KLA, in its propaganda, was very anxious to proclaim that it really was an army?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: My guess is you could say that, but from what we saw on the ground, they were in uniforms and they certainly -- for the use of the protocol II standards, they certainly met the test of being an organised armed force.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Let's be a little careful here shall we, Mr. Bouckaert?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: When you say "we," at the point in which you were there in September and again in November, you observed people in uniform. How many of them did you meet?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: We met KLA soldiers and commanders on almost a daily basis. It would be difficult to -- sometimes we'd meet significant groups of KLA soldiers, so it would be very difficult to estimate over that period of six weeks exactly how many we met.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I appreciate that. Again, the dangers of extrapolating backwards from your experience towards the end of the year to how things were earlier in the year, the middle of the year, I'm sure you would make allowances there certainly.

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, I would make allowances between what I directly observed and the analytical contribution I made to the preparation of the Humanitarian Law Violations in Kosovo report, which was based on the research of my colleague as well as other documentation available to us, but that was also part of the preparation of that report during July and August, late July and August.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: There is no question but that people flocked to the KLA, seeking to join, shortly after the massacres in Drenica. We have already established that.

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: The question of how much ability the KLA had to organise those people, provide them with uniforms, provide them even with weapons is again we're back in a fluid situation, aren't we?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And that many of those folks were simply, as you said, farmers who showed up with their hunting rifles. You didn't say that, I'm putting that to you. But they were farmers and many, of course, would have had hunting rifles as part of their ordinary daily lives.

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were farmers who joined, and some did carry old hunting rifles, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Did they have -- did they turn up with any other more makeshift weapons, farming implements, as far as you were informed, pitchforks and the like?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I saw. Most of the -- by the time I arrived in Kosovo certainly most people were in uniform and generally had Kalashnikov weapons, although occasionally we would see people with older weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I guess by the time --

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No pitchforks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: That's by the time you arrived.

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, as I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I'm very grateful to you, Mr. Bouckaert. Thank you very much. Give me regards to Reed Brody when you see him.

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: No questions from the Prosecution, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, Mr. Bouckaert, that is the end of the questions, it seems, for you. Thank you very much for your attendance and assistance. Sorry you were delayed over the weekend, and you may now, of course, leave and go about your other interests.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Prosecution is prepared with its next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please read the affirmation on the card that is offered to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, I will. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Would you please state your name.

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: My name is Zeqir Gashi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, sir, can you understand me through the interpreter all right?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I can understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I would just ask you to, when listening to my questions, that you take your time to listen to the entire question before responding. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And if at any time you do not understand the interpretation or you do not understand my question, please tell me. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, could you tell us your date of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: 29th of March, 1963.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I was born in Lapusnik village, in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you go to school in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I went there during the first four years of primary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Where did you go to school after that?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I continued the other four years until the eighth grade in Komorane.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And after you went to school in Komorane, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I went to the high school in Gllogovc.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And after that did you continue your education?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you tell us what --

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I continued my studies at Pristina university.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What did you study there?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Initially I studied chemistry for a year. Then I transferred to the faculty of medicine.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you tell us what years you studied at Pristina University.

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I studied from 1983 to 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you become a doctor at the end of those [microphone not activated]?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I finished my studies but I was not given a diploma because at the time, we were not given diplomas at the faculty of medicine in Albanian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you explain for us, please?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: From the 1980s, all the faculties of Albanian university were subjected to violent measures, so we were obliged to continue the studies in a parallel system in private clinics, in private homes. Because the facilities of the faculties generally were occupied by the Serb occupiers, and the students, Albanian students and professors didn't have access to such institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So could you tell us what years you were in this parallel system of study?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: From 1989 to 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What kind of medicine did you study during those years, both in the faculty and in this parallel system of private clinics and private homes that you've described?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: General medicine. I didn't practice any particular medical specialty.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And the parallel -- parallel system that you've described from 1989 to 1993, was that also in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes, it was in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: After you completed those studies both at the faculty and what you've described as the parallel studies, the parallel system, in 1993, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I don't understand the question well. You mean in 1993 or after 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes. I'll rephrase it, and I apologise; it wasn't a very clear question. In 1993, after you finished your studies, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I had a private clinic my own home in the village where I could meet my material needs to some extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And which village was this?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: In Lapusnik village.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was it in the home that you grew up in that you had this private clinic?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If you're driving on the Pristina-Peja road and you're driving towards Peja, is your house located on the right-hand side of the road or on the left-hand side of the road in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: My house is located on the right-hand side of the road, some 300 metres away from the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Drawing your attention to May of 1998, were you still working at that clinic at your home in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Around the 8th or 9th of May, did something happen?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: The first battle between the Kosovo Liberation Army and the Serb police started in the Lapusnik forest.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Where were you whether that fighting started?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I was in my village. I was at my home.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What did you do when the fighting started?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Nothing. We found some accommodation, then we took our families away in safer places in other villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Where did you take your family?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I took my family to Pokleku village where my wife had her family.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you describe for us where that village is?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: This village is situated in the vicinity of the municipal centre of Gllogovc, some two or three kilometres south of Gllogovc.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Pokleku village?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I stayed that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what happened the next day?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: On the next day I returned to my own house because everything we had was there and I went there to take care of our property.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How long did you stay -- this is your house in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes. I stayed there about two weeks, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what did you do after those two weeks? What happened?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: During these two weeks, there were attacks by Serb forces, police forces situated in Komorane. After two weeks they started to shell with heavy artillery, and then it was unsafe for us to remain there in our houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The shelling with heavy artillery, do you know where that came from, where the shelling was from?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: The shelling came from Komorane where the Serb forces had their headquarters or had their base.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What did you do when the shelling began?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: We went to Orlat village, which was close by, a few kilometres away from our village, away from the Serb positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court what direction Orlat is in relation to Lapusnik.

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Orlat is some five kilometres west of Lapusnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When you went to Orlat, where did you stay?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I stayed at the house of one of my cousins.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was your family still in Pokleku village at this time?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: No. They continued their trip to another village. Gllogovc e Eperm, to another municipality, because of safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So they were not with you in Orlat?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: No. No, they were not with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, after you moved to Orlat, was there more fighting in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: To my recollection, there were fighting on the 28th or the 29th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Where were you when this fighting occurred on the 28th or 29th of May?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I was in Orlat village.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: After the 28th or 29th of May, did you return -- have occasion to return to Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I returned to Lapusnik, but not to the place where our houses were situated.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Where in Lapusnik did you return to?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: We returned to that part which was not the target of the Serb forces, to that part which lies south of the west -- of the road Pristina-Peja.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What was your reason for returning to Lapusnik at this time?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: The reason why I returned to Lapusnik at that time was to offer my medical services to the population that was left behind in that area in order for me to help them as much as I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What did you do to provide medical services to the population?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: First I contacted Ymer Alushani with whom I discussed what we could do to open a medical clinic to provide medical assistance to the population that had remained there. He introduced me to one of the leaders of the KLA there by the pseudonym of Qerqizi. And sometime at the beginning of June, we opened that clinic, which was a makeshift one, I have to say, improvised one.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did Ymer Alushani tell you why he wanted to introduce you to Qerqiz?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Because, as far as I remember or understood, Qerqiz was the leader of the unit that was in Lapusnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you know the name of the unit that was in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: The name was Celiku.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you remember when you learned that that was the name of the unit?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly when.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you remember if it was -- do you remember approximately when?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: At the beginning that we opened the clinic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you testified that you opened the clinic sometime at the beginning of June; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Where was the clinic in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: The clinic was opened in the house of Mr. Ferat Sopi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You mentioned somebody by the name of Ymer Alushani. Did you know Ymer Alushani before the war?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him also before the war. We went to primary school together, but we were not of the same generation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you know Ymer Alushani's pseudonym at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: His pseudonym was Voglushi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: At the clinic did you work by yourself or with others?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I did not work by myself. We had two nurses.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How long - and I mean in terms of days or months or weeks or -- but how long did you work at that clinic in Lapusnik? Until when?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: In this clinic in Lapusnik, we worked every day from the beginning until that part of the territory fell on the Serb occupation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you remember when that happened, when the territory fell to the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: It was the 25th or the 26th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you describe the work that you did at the clinic, please.

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: In general, we provided service to all, but mostly we had to deal with the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Approximately how many people would you treat each day?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: We treated approximately 20, 25 people a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And was that figure true from the beginning until the end?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I'm talking about an average number of people. Some days we treated more, some days we treated less.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But did that average hold true for the entire period, from the beginning of June until the end of July?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: This is an approximate figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You said you treated civilians. Did you also treat soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: We treated soldiers as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: With regard to both civilians and soldiers, what kinds of medical problems did you treat? Could you just give me a kind of list of the types of problems.

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: We treated all kinds of medical problems the civilian populations had -- population had. In the case of soldiers, we treated some injuries, slight injuries, and especially the allergies which were very widespread at that time. And some people who might have had chronic problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What kinds of chronic problems would you treat?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Blood pressure, high blood pressure, then other diseases like lung diseases, chronic lung diseases which were prevalent among the population, and such kind of diseases.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When you treated the soldiers, would you talk to them?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes, usually we did. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know if all the soldiers were from Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I don't know, because our duty was to provide medical assistance to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If you were faced with serious -- a serious medical problem, what would you do?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: We would advise them to go to other places where they might receive the adequate treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Where were such other places?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: In Malishev municipal centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And specifically what was located in Malishev that people could go to if they faced a serious medical problem?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. Can you repeat it? Can you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, I can. What was located in Malishev? Where would you send them to in Malishev?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: There was a clinic there which existed for a long time. It had medical personnel who were specialised to treat more serious problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you describe for us a little bit the conditions you worked under during June and July of 1998 in the clinic in Lapusnik. What were the conditions like?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: The conditions were not the ideal ones. That facility, per se, was a makeshift one, as I said. We had a quantity of medicaments, medical supplies, to provide first aid. That was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What kind of hours did you work?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Usually we worked from morning to 5.00, 6.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you sleep in Lapusnik or did you sleep somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Usually I slept at the house of my cousin in Orlat.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher I'm going to show you an aerial image. It's tab 4 of the bundle, and it's image 8 from P001, but this particular one has been marked. No, if we could put it on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And, sir, if you could look at that image now. It's on what we call the ELMO, to your left. It's better if you took at it on the -- to your left rather than on the computer. Do you -- do you recognise that?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Have you seen this image before?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes. I have seen that during the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to draw your attention the lower right of the page, on the white margin. Do you see a signature there?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes, it's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, it's a little bit hard to see, but to the right of the -- of the well-marked red circle there's another red circle. Maybe the -- maybe the -- we could zoom in a little bit on the ELMO. Do you see, sir, that red circle there?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What is that?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'll rephrase it. Did you make that mark during the interview?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what is inside of that red circle that you drew?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: It's the place where the clinic was located.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, can you describe, or maybe if you could be given the pointer could you show where -- how you would get from the clinic to Orlat.

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Along this road you could go to the clinic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to be -- I'm going to ask that you be given a pen, and if you could just draw a line on that road.

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I see that there are two Xs along that road that you've drawn that were previously on this diagram. Did you put those two Xs on this image during your interview?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What do those two Xs represent?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: They were two checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And who operated those checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Usually they were operated by KLA soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you just mark -- draw over those two Xs, just draw the X again over it so it's more clearly visible.

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you have to pass through those checkpoints when you travelled to and from Orlat?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you require any kind of a pass or permission to go through those checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: No, I didn't require anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know if soldiers required passes or permissions when they travelled outside of Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I am not sure, but I heard that they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you remember who you heard that from?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I don't remember who I heard that from.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you remember if you heard that from soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I believe so, but I don't know from whom of them I heard it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand. We're finished with that image.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And if it could be given a number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be Prosecution Exhibit 213.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Whiting, is that a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I was just going to ask. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will break now. We must interrupt your evidence, Doctor, to rewind the tapes. We will break for 20 minutes and resume at five minutes past four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, when you were at this clinic, working at the clinic in Lapusnik during June and July of 1998, where would you get food?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your answer was not picked up because the microphones weren't on. If you could give your answer again, please.

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: We would eat in the kitchen, which was a joint kitchen for all of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you remember where that kitchen was?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. It was in the house of Mr. Gzim Gashi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You said it was "a joint kitchen for all of us." For all of whom?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: For us who worked in the clinic but also for the soldiers. They had their meals there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, I'm going to show you a photograph. It's from P006. It's on page 18 and it's ERN number U0083683. And if it could be placed on the ELMO, please. Doctor, if you could look at that image, please, that's to your left.

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recognise the buildings in that image?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: This is the house of Gzim Gashi where the kitchen was located.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is the house of the Gzim Gashi one of the buildings, one particular building in this image?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you take a pen and just put an X on the building that is the house of Gzim Gashi.

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: There is a mark but just -- since it's maybe hard to see, if the record could reflect that it's on the yellow building which is on the very left of the image. I think the witness is being given another better pen to make the marking. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And if this image could be given a number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Prosecution Exhibit P214.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And it can be taken off the ELMO. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Doctor, before the break you testified that you saw Qerqiz before you were introduced by Ymer Alushani, and you saw him before you set up this clinic at the beginning of June. Did you see him again in Lapusnik, that is Qerqiz?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: If you could repeat the question. It's not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It was a very long, confusing question. My question was: Did you see Qerqiz again in Lapusnik after the beginning of June?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I did see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: During June and July of 1998, how often did you see him?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I could have seen him probably every second day or every third day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: During June and July of 1998, what did you think Qerqiz's position was in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I believe that he was the leader of the unit in Lapusnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Doctor, when you needed medical supplies, what would you do?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: When we needed medical supplies, we would compile a list with things that we required, and then we would hand this list to Qerqiz, and through him we would get the medical supplies that we needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How often did that happen in June and July?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I don't know how often, but whenever there was a need for us to do a request, we did so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you tell us approximately how many times that happened? Was it once a week, once every other week, once a month?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I can't say anything about it because I don't know exactly. It could be once a week. It could be more frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: After you gave the list of supplies that you needed to Qerqiz, what happened? What would happen?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Usually after some time they would bring us the supplies.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Who would bring you the supplies?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Some of the soldiers, even Qerqiz himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: During June and July of 1998, do you know where Qerqiz stayed in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. He could have stayed in the area of Ferat Sopi's compound. What makes you think that he could have stayed in the area of Ferat Sopi's compound?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
