utterances.text: I saw him frequently there in the neighbourhood, and he would sometimes come to the clinic and ask us if we needed anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, when you say -- you testified that you believed he was the leader of the unit in Lapusnik.

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can -- can you be more clear about what that meant? What was the unit in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I don't understand the questions -- question. Could you be a little bit more specific, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes. I'll rephrase my question. Was he the leader of all of the soldiers in Lapusnik or some of the soldiers in Lapusnik, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: To my understanding, he was the leader of the entire unit in Lapusnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, did -- while you were in Lapusnik in June and July of 1998, were new soldiers joining the KLA, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I did see new faces, but I don't know whether they were new soldiers or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know anything about how new soldiers would join the KLA in Lapusnik? Did you hear anything about that? Did you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I heard that Qerqiz would interview them, and then after that they would join or not join the KLA ranks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you hear anything about Qerqiz's reputation as a commander in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I didn't hear anything bad about him. On the contrary, I heard good words about him from the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What kinds of good words did you hear about him?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: That he was a good leader, that he treated soldiers well, words like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you ever treat Qerqiz at the clinic?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I think I treated him once in the clinic for a minor injury in his arm.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did Qerqiz have a beard in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you describe the beard, please.

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: In what way should I describe his beard?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, first the size of the beard. Was it a big beard, a small beard?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: To my recollection, he had a big beard.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you ever learn the real name of Qerqiz?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: No. During that time in Lapusnik, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you learn it later?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I learnt it here when the proceedings started here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What did you learn his real name to be?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Isak Musliu.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: During the last week before you left Lapusnik at the end of July, did you see Qerqiz?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I don't know. To tell you the truth, five years have passed since then, so I cannot tell you exactly whether I've seen him or not. Perhaps I did see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But you're not sure?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: While you were at Lapusnik during June and July of 1998, did you hear of a person with the name Celiku?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I have heard it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What did you hear about this person with the name Celiku?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I heard that he was one of the KLA commanders, that he was a brave young man.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you hear anything about where he commanded or what he commanded?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I heard that he was a commander in Klecka.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And did you hear what area he commanded?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: No. I don't know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you -- did you see -- did you ever meet Celiku?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I have seen Celiku. I've met him in Lapusnik. During his visit, he came to the clinic, he asked us if we needed anything, how things were going in the clinic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How many times did that happen?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: To my recollection, twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you ever see Celiku with Qerqiz?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I've seen them once in front of our clinic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you know what the relationship was between Celiku and Qerqiz?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When -- did you learn Celiku's real name?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes. I learned Celiku's real name during that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What's "that time"?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: During my stay in Lapusnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What did you learn his real name to be?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Fatmir Limaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you remember how you learned that to be his name?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I learned his name from the people I worked with.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you ever hear about an oath ceremony in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I did hear about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How did you hear about it?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I heard about it from Ymer Alushani.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: He told me that the oath ceremony took place sometime in June and that Celiku held a speech. I don't know the content of this speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was Ymer Alushani at the oath ceremony, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know where the oath ceremony was held?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: It was held somewhere in Lapusnik, though I don't know exactly where.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know approximately where?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you ever hear anything about Celiku's reputation?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I heard good words only.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What kinds of good words?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: That he was a good commander, that he was a brave man and a wise man.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What did you think his role was in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Are you sure?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I am sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you know anything about his command, Celiku's command?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I knew - I mean everyone knew that Celiku was a commander, but as to what his role was, I don't know, and I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But I mean, you say everyone knew that he was a commander. Commander of what?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Commander of KLA units, but what his role was precisely, it wasn't our duty to learn these roles.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm not asking about his role precisely, I'm just asking what you believed his area of command to be. What did you think was included in his area of command?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I heard that he was a commander in Klecka. Now, if any other zone fell under his command, I didn't know of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know if Lapusnik fell under his command?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Considering the name Celiku, it can fall under his command, but now ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you have any other reason to think that Lapusnik fell under his command? Your conversations with soldiers, for example.

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let me move to another topic. Did you know a person by the name of Haradin Bala in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you know him before the war?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him from before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How did you know him?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: The village Haradin comes from is the village that my mother comes from.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What village is that? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: It is Koretica e Larte village.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How long had you known him before the war?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: It was probably ten to 15 years that I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you know anything about Haradin Bala's father?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Everyone in Drenica knew his father. He was a well-known singer of folk songs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: During June and July of 1998, did you see Haradin Bala in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Objection, leading. He can ask him what times he saw him, but he's leading him to an answer at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's hard, Your Honour, to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Just carry on. Whatever harm there is has been done, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you see Haradin Bala in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When did you see him in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: He came to our clinic once or twice for a check-up.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But when was it in terms of time period?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: During the time we stayed in Lapusnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you be more clear; what months?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: June and July 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Solely for purposes of the record, I think the Chamber has already acknowledged the damage has already been done so I question the advocacy or the validity or the weight, or for that matter, weight that this answer can be given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber's comment, Mr. Guy-Smith, was to the effect of whatever harm there may have been is already done. It was not that there had been harm done.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I take it a step further, then, that the harm has been done.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You said that he came to the clinic for a check-up. Do you remember what happened at the check-up, or the check-ups?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: He usually complained for high blood pressure and arrhythmic heartbeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So what would you do at the check-up?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Usually we took his blood pressure, listened to his heart and advised him of his medical condition. If we had medicaments, then we would prescribe them to him and give it to him, and if we didn't, then we would recommend the ones that he was supposed to take.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Aside from at the clinic, did you see him anywhere else in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Once or twice on our way to the kitchen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly, but it was within this period when we stayed in Lapusnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And is this period June and July of 1998?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know if Haradin Bala had a pseudonym?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes. His pseudonym was Shala.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know what his duties were in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I think he was an ordinary soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you describe how he looked at that time.

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: He was of medium height. He wore a moustache. This is to what extent I can describe him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Aside from his complaints of high blood pressure and arrythmia, do you remember anything else about his physical condition, his health?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you ever send him to the hospital in Malisevo, to your memory?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you remember anything about the medicaments that you prescribed to him?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, I want to draw your attention to -- Doctor, to September of 2003. Do you remember meeting with an investigator from the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was that the first time that you had met with somebody from the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes, it was the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Doctor, did the investigator ask you questions about Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you sign a statement?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: No, I didn't sign a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Doctor, were you truthful to the investigator?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Partly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Does that mean that partly you were not truthful?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you remember what you were not truthful about?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I wasn't truthful because I didn't want to get involved in these trial proceedings as a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And do you remember what subjects you were not truthful about?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do apologise. Can I just check the date of this statement. Is it September 2003 or February 2005?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's not a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: It's an interview with the investigator.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And it is September 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Before my learned friend proceeds, may I ask if any document has been produced as a result of that meeting in September of 2003?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, and it was disclosed to the Defence on the 26th of November, 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: I'm very grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Doctor, if I could continue my questions. Do you remember what subjects you were not truthful about in that first meeting with the investigator of the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: To my recollection, I did say that I know Mr. Haradin Bala.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction: I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And was that true?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: No, that was not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And do you remember if you were asked questions about Celiku and Qerqiz?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, drawing your attention to the 23rd and 24th of February of this year, 2005, were you again interviewed by somebody from the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And was this the second time you had been interviewed?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes, it was the second time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you sign a statement this time?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I did sign one.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were you truthful?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Why did you tell the truth on this second occasion?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: It is true that on the second occasion I did say that my time in Lapusnik was a public -- something that I did in public, not in secret. Everybody knew that I was there at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But what changed? Why on the first occasion you did not tell the truth completely and then on the second occasion you did tell the truth? Why did that change?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: During the conversation we had with the investigator on the second occasion, I emphasised to the investigator that nobody wants to be a witness, especially not in a case dealing with crimes. The reason I changed my statement was that the truth comes to surface sooner or later, and I have nothing to hide.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Are you telling the truth today?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to object to that. That's a determination for the Chamber to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think in the circumstances it's a very proper question, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Doctor, are you telling the truth today?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we go into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Doctor, this person that we were just talking about, how often did you see him in Lapusnik after the beginning of June 1998?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I met him quite frequently. I cannot speak in numbers. He would come to the clinic from time to time when we had no work to do, and we would play chess.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know what his duties were in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I believe he was an ordinary soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: After Lapusnik fell at the end of July 1998, did you see him again?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I met him once or twice in Fshati i Ri or Novosel it was called then. We had again an improvised or makeshift clinic in the facility of the village school there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you remember the occasions that you met him? What happened, or why did you meet him?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I think that he had an inflammation and he came for a check-up. We prescribed him some medicine.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, turning back to the time that you were working at the clinic in Lapusnik in June and July of 1998, did you on occasion write prescriptions?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Usually we did write prescriptions in loose paper, white paper, because there was no other way to write them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, I'm going to show you the documents which are at tab 6 of our bundle. ERN U0087691 to 7702. It's tab 6, for the usher. If you could look at those pages there. There are --

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recognise those?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I do recognise them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What are they?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: These are the names of our patients, the diagnosis, and the prescribed therapy.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know who wrote these?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I wrote them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is that your signature on the bottom of these -- of each page?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And are these from the time in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes. They have the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd ask that these be given a number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 6 would be Prosecution Exhibit P215.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, were medical records -- were records of -- well, medical records also kept at your clinic during June and July of 1998?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Whose responsibility was it to keep the records?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Usually the nurses kept the records.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to turn to tab 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Maybe the usher could assist the witness to look at the documents which are at tab 5. And for the record, those are ERN U0087665 to 7768.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: This is a notebook which is called "Dressing Station," and if you could just take a moment to turn the pages and look at the entries. Now, is this your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recognise the handwriting?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I do not recognise the handwriting. There were two or three other persons who could have written this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recognise the names in the book?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: If I could read them, yes, I do recognise the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And how do you recognise the names?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Most of them are with the family name of Gashi and Sopi. Then we have some pseudonyms of the soldiers. And people with this family name usually come from our village.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you see the dates that are listed?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Are those dates consistent with the time that you were in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: They are consistent, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is this record of dressings or bandages consistent with the kinds of records that were kept at your clinic?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Some are consistent and some are illegible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is it your testimony that the ones that you can read are consistent?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: It seems to me that they are consistent.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd ask that this document be given a number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 5 will be Prosecution Exhibit P216.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Finally, Doctor, I'd ask you to turn to tab 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Maybe the usher could assist the witness with that also. And the ERN, for the record, is U0087723 to 7728.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, could you take a moment to look at this record. And if you could look at the -- I don't know if you're looking at the Albanian version. Yes, you are. And this is called "List of injections." Is this your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recognise the names in this document?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise these names. These are the names of people from the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Are the dates consistent with the dates that you were working at the clinic in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes, they are consistent.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And is this record consistent with the kinds of records that were kept at your clinic?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: It seems to me that it is consistent.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this document be given a number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 7 will be Prosecution Exhibit P217.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Doctor, I'm going to move to another subject. Did you ever hear about a prison in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you ever visit a prison in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You've spoken about Gzim Gashi's house where you went for food. Was there a compound across the road from Gzim Gashi's compound?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I think there are other houses apart from Gzim's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Specifically across the road. Are there other houses or compounds across the road from Gzim's house?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I think there are.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you ever go into the compound that is across the road from Gzim's compound?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I had no reason to go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you see other people going in or out of that compound?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: There were occasions when I did see other people going there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you see -- were these other people soldiers or civilians, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Soldiers and civilians, but it seems that every house at that time in Lapusnik served as a shelter and a place for the soldiers to stay, because to my understanding, there were no other places for them to stay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to draw your attention to the end of July, when you've already testified that Lapusnik fell. Do you remember the date that the attack happened on Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I remember it was early in the morning of 25th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Where were you when the attack started?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I was in Orlat village, and later I went to Lapusnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When you went to Lapusnik, where did you go in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I went to the location where the clinic was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: The entire morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did the attack continue?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: It continued, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What did you do at the end of the morning?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: We tried to take the medicine, the medicaments from that house to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. another house which was a little bit further from the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was that house still in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes, it was in Lapusnik, but further from the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In which direction in relation to the Ferat Sopi house was that house, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I think it was west of that house.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How long did you stay in that house?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: We stayed there 'til the next day, when we left Lapusnik and fled to the mountains.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: We took some mountain roads and stayed in the village which is up in the Berisha mountains, and after that we went to Novosel or Fshati i Ri.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Just to be clear, what is the name of the village that is up in the Berisha mountains that you went to?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: The name in Albanian is Fshati i Ri. At that time it was called Novosel.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: After you left Lapusnik, what's the first village that you went to?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Berisha. We didn't stay there. We went on towards Novosel.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How long did it take for you to get from Lapusnik to Berisha?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: About two to three hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you go by yourself or were there others making that same trip?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I went with the nurses who assisted me in my work.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And did you see other people also making this trip?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I saw other people making the same trip, villagers and some soldiers as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to Ymer Alushani?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: He was killed on that day in Lapusnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You said that you went to Novosel after Berisha. How long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: We stayed there from the end of July when we arrived up to the early September.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And I believe you've already said a little bit about what you were doing, but could you tell us what exactly you were doing during that time period in Novosel.

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: During the time in Novosel, we reopened the clinic with the help of some other nurses from that village and continued to provide medical assistance to the local population that -- whose number had grown as a result of the incoming population from the surrounding villages. They amounted to some 50, 60.000 of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: During that time period, how many people did you treat each day?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: We treated a very, very large number of people. It happened that we might treat up to 200 people a day. But we were in a better position than before thanks to the assistance we received from Doctors Without Borders, who provided us with more medicaments that we could provide to the local population.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: After you left Lapusnik, did you see Qerqiz again?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I didn't see him again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you see Celiku again?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I met him once. He came to the clinic, and he asked us, as usual, how things were with us, whether we were providing the necessary medical assistance to the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you remember when that was?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: To my recollection, it was by mid-August or the first half of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: At the beginning of September of 1998, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: From Novosel, after shelling by the occupation forces started against Novosel, personally I went to the valley between Kishna Reka and Berisha where there was an enormous number of displaced people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I stayed there for about -- from the early September up to the 17th, 18th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Where did you go after that?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: From there we -- I decided to go to Pristina to visit my family, and then I continued my trip to Shale. There is another village there. South of Kishna Reka village, from there, through some other villages, I went to Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did there come an occasion when you were arrested by the Serb authorities?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you remember when that happened?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Three or four days after my arrival in Pristina. They came and arrested me in the house of my father.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know why you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I do not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did -- was --

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Can you be more specific, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Did they give you a reason for your arrest by the Serbs? Did they give you a reason why they were arresting you?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: When the arrest took place, it was a kind of kidnapping, I would say. They didn't have a reason to give me why they were arresting me. After -- afterwards, they took me to the premises of the Serb security, and there they started to interrogate me and to maltreat and to debase me mercilessly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Doctor, how long were you held by the Serb authorities?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Four days.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: After your release, did you stay in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I stayed in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you -- and I don't want you to say where you went, but did there come a time when you left Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes. I left Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you live in another country now?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Are you working in that country? Please don't say --

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I work.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Are you working as a doctor?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: No, I don't work as a doctor, because to work as a doctor I need a licence, and I'm working for that. I'm doing another job.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What year did you leave Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: In the spring of 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You said that in the country where you're living now that you're working for that, the licence. Do you hope one day to work as a doctor again?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I hope that in the near future I will be able to work as a doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. I don't have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: My name is Gregor Guy-Smith, and along with Mr. Harvey I represent Haradin Bala, a man who you know, correct?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The reason that you know Haradin Bala is that your family and his family come from the same village, true?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I take it that before the war you have been to his home. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I haven't been to his home, but we have met.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say you've met, you've met in the village; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: How close is your family's home to Mr. Bala's home, in the village?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Do you mean the village where I used to live and the village where Mr. Bala lived?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, the village where your -- where your -- I believe it was where your mother came from; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Correct. It is half a kilometre away.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Before the war in the '90s and in 1990 and 1991, 1992, and 1993, that was a time in which, as I understand it, you were in the process of studying for purposes of becoming a doctor; right?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And you were denied -- you were denied your ability to obtain a degree because of the behaviour of the Serbs, and you've described the parallel education system that you went through in order to continue your studies; right?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, during that time, and I'm referring to the early years in 1990, did you have occasion to see Haradin Bala during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes, either in his village or in Komorane where usually on Saturdays there is a marketplace.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the marketplace in Komorane is -- on Saturdays is a place where people from a variety of different villages gather; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, in 1993 through 19 let's say hundred and ninety-seven, did you have an opportunity to see Mr. Bala during that time?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I could meet him, maybe not very often.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And everybody -- everybody in the community knew that you were studying to be a doctor and as a matter of fact had some expertise in that regard; right?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: People would come and ask you for advice, true? Even before you were able to open your clinic; right?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes. Sometimes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Were you aware of the fact that in 1993 and times thereafter that Haradin Bala had suffered at least one if not a number of heart attacks? That information was discussed with you?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I think that during the time he came to me for a check-up in Lapusnik we discussed the cause for his arrythmia, which was his heart condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Before the check-up in Lapusnik is the time that I'm now concerned about, Dr. Gashi. Before that time, you were aware, weren't you, that Haradin Bala suffered from a heart condition; right?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware before -- I wasn't aware that he was suffering from that disease.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: During the time that you spoke with him and you learned about his heart history, what information did you obtain from him at that time at this check-up that you had with him?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: What do you mean by the word "information"?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, did you get a medical history from him, get some kind of understanding of what had been going on with him historically so you were in a position of -- to make, I guess if not a diagnosis a prognosis of how he was doing?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: To my recollection, we discussed a little bit, but we didn't go into details.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, as you sit here today, the little bit that you discussed, do you have any independent memory of what you discussed with him?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: The only thing that I remember very well is that he had arrythmia and that he showed me the medicaments he was using, and we took his blood pressure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: What kind of medicine was he taking at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I try to remember. It was beta blocker or some other medicaments.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And what's a beta blocker? What does that do?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: They regulate the work of the heart in case of arrythmia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you -- do you recall whether he was taking one medicine or a number of different kinds of medicines at the time that you had this check-up with him?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Maybe he was taking other medicaments, but this is the only medicine I remember he was taking then.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you prescribe him any medicines at that time for the condition that he was apparently at least complaining about if not suffering from?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I am not sure whether I prescribed something to him or I gave, actually gave something because maybe we had something there in the clinic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, when people came to see you at the clinic before May 1998, at that time did you keep records of each patient that came to see you?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Usually we did keep records.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And -- and after May of 1998, when you opened the clinic, during that period of time I take it that one of the things that you also did, because it's good medical practice, is to keep records of those people who came to see you; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Excuse me. If I could just object. The -- well, I think the question misstates the evidence. The clinic was opened after the beginning of June 1998 is the evidence, not after May 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We'll get to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, as a matter of fact, when you were having a discussion sometime in 2003 with the investigator, as I understand it you've indicated that you were untruthful about one thing, as I understood it, which was whether or not you knew Mr. Bala, but you were truthful about other things. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you were speaking to the investigator, I'm referring to, I believe it's page 3 of Mr. Tucker's notes, you told the investigator that you based yourself at the location from around May 1998 and remained until the end of July, around the 25th of July; right?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I think I said early June until the 25th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you met with the investigator, did you have a chance to look over the notes that he took?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Were those notes read to you in Albanian or read to you in English? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Excuse me. If we could just get clarification on which interview you're talking about now, because the question was just when you met with the investigator, and there are two separate interviews.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure. Not a problem. I'm referring to the interview that was taken by Mr. Tucker, which I believe is the 2003 interview, the one which he did not sign.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In that interview when you met with -- do you remember meeting with Mr. Tucker from the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And during that time when you met with Mr. Tucker - just we'll back up here for a minute - he asked you a series of questions, including -- he asked you where you were based in terms of where the clinic was; right?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And you told him where you were based. You told him that you were based in a local house in a compound in Lapusnik; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You also at that time told him that the local population knew that you were in the area and mainly people used to come and see you and the nurses in the house; right? You told him that?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I've told that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You also told him that you travelled to see elderly people or other kinds of folks who were not able to come to the clinic to meet you; right?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes. And other people who couldn't make it to the clinic, we went ourselves to check them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You told him you didn't have very many medical supplies but what you did have you got from volunteer organisations; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Correct. From voluntary organisations. In rare occasions we got supplies from the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And now with regard to the dates in which you're referring to, I'm going to read what the notes say and see whether that helps you in terms of remembering what you told the investigator at the time. You told the investigator that you based yourself at the location, that location being the local house, the compound, Lapusnik, from around May 1998 and remained until the end of July. Around the 25th of July when the Serbs commenced their offensive of the village, at that time the population of Lapusnik fled into the surrounding mountains and you fled with them. That's what you told the investigator at that time, and my concern right now really is the issue of the date, which is you started your efforts trying to help the population working as a doctor in May, starting around May; right?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I started to help the population. I have never ceased trying. First in my own home during the time we stayed there. After we left home, then we, as I said, opened that clinic in the southern part of Lapusnik where we stayed until July, 25th of July, when we left the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I appreciate that. The importance is when you began that. That clinic -- that clinic, I didn't -- I didn't mean to interrupt you. That clinic was at the home of Ferat Sopi; right?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And that's a clinic that I'm suggesting to you, as you told Mr. Tucker, the investigator, when you met with him in 2003 and you were telling the truth, is a clinic that you opened in May. Right?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Maybe it's a mistake, because this clinic was open in the beginning of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know somebody by the name of Nazif Sopi?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I know him. He is from Lapusnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And Nazif Sopi is related to Ferat Sopi; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I believe they must be cousins.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you know an individual named Cercin or Kercin Sopi?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Maybe you mean Cirkin Sopi?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's who I meant, yes. So I assume by you correcting me you obviously know the individual.

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I know that individual. I knew him at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'd like you to go back, if I could with the help of the usher, to what has now been admitted as P213, which is the aerial map.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. If you could put it on the ELMO, that would be lovely.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Taking a look at this -- at this document, Doctor, and once again going back to the area where you had previously made a circle, that's the area which I believe you've told us is where the clinic was located; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could you, using if you have a darker pen, specifically circle the home of Ferat Sopi in that area, which I believe is what you've designated as being the clinic. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I can't see it clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In looking at where you have drawn the previous circle, are you able to approximate where Ferat Sopi's home would be and point to it, other than the large circle that you've drawn that covers somewhat of an area?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: It may be here somewhere, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And you've -- you've drawn I think a blue circle around -- around that; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I don't know how much longer you wish to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: This is just about the moment. I was waiting to see whether you were moving on or tidying something up.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm about to take a breath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will then have the second break at this moment, resuming at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: During the time that you were in Lapusnik during the summer of 1998, did you have occasion to go to Nazif Sopi's home?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I have passed nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And if you were to once again, looking at the ELMO, looking at the map 2 -- the area map of 213, are you able to identify where Nazif Sopi's home would be on that map or on that -- I really should say photographic view, aerial view?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: It might be north-west of Ferat's home.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Using -- using the pointer initially, could you point it -- point it out for us on the map?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Here, in this vicinity.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could you put an NS in the area that you've indicated, indicating the area which Nazif Sopi's home would be.

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to the home of the individual whose name I mangled before, which I believe was Qerkin Sopi - hopefully I've done better this time - looking once again at that map, are you able to identify where Qerkin Sopi's home would be; and if you can, could you kindly put the letters QS, indicating where that individual's home would be.

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I can't tell it very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's fine. That's okay. During the summer of 1998, did you have occasion to visit Qerkin Sopi's home?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I might have, because it was nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, I want to go back for a moment and discuss the -- the manner of not only keeping records but also what you did when patients came in to see you at the clinic. Okay?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, by the -- by the time that you were working at the clinic in Lapusnik in the summer of 1998, you had been seeing patients for some period of time; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: What do you think I had been seeing patients for some period of time? I'm not clear about the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, people had come -- people had come to see you and asked for your medical assistance for some period of time, for some time before you began working in this clinic, as you've described it to us, at Lapusnik.

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the procedure that you used at that time before the -- the clinic that you opened in Lapusnik, the procedure that you used at that time is that when a patient came to see you, you took some kind of notes, some kind of medical history about them, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes. As is usual in such cases, you take data related to their medical history.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The reason that you take the data related to the medical history is so that you have a record of whatever complaints or observations you may have made of a particular patient so that you have some way of checking up to see what's happened with them, what their history is; right?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes. This is what one usually does.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And you've told us that you were treating people for such things as allergies or lung ailments or other chronic conditions during the time that you were at Lapusnik during the summer of 1998; right?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When one of those individuals would come in, for example, somebody who had a lung condition, when they would come in you would take a medical history from that person so that you would have a basis upon which to make a determination of what an appropriate course of treatment would be; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's good medical practice; right?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yeah, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to any kind of medications that you would prescribe to the individual or any medical advice that you would give to the individual, you would make notations of that, too, would you not?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes. We usually make notations about that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And there's a specific reason for making those kinds of notations because when you've administered a medication to a person for a particular condition you want to know what kind of success that medication might be having; right?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the documents we've discussed here today, I don't know if you have them in front of you, and that would be people's -- P215.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If the usher could give him, please, P215.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I believe if you -- if you'd take a look at -- if I'm not mistaken, it's U0087691. The only thing I'm trying to determine there, the notation there is for the 19th of February; correct? That's when you saw that particular individual; right? That would be Gjule Gashi?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes, it says 19 July 1998. If you look more closer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. With regard to -- let me ask you about another notation, and I believe it is on page U0087700. I believe that that's -- the date is the 22nd of March, at which point you saw Shaban Gashi. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: It seems so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, also with regard to the -- the notation concerning Shaban Gashi, there's some numbers there. I believe it's 3754/7. Do you know what those numbers signify?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Must be the number of the patient, as far as I can make it out here. The month.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The number of the patient for that month?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I am not sure whether it's the number of the patient for that particular month or the total number of patients until that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. You certainly had some kind of system whereby you would be able to determine the number of patients that you'd seen as you've told us you gave us an average of the number of patients you'd seen, but you had an internal system to note the number of patients you'd seen; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Usually we kept notes on a book, on a notebook. Do you mean by an internal rule or system?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure, some internal rule or system. And the internal system contained a couple of things; it contained the patient's name, the date you saw the patient, and perhaps the number that patient was, meaning where that patient stood in the number of patients you had already seen either for that date or for that month or collectively in entirety, as well as some indication of what the patient was doing there; right? Somebody complained of being -- having a hard time breathing. Somebody might complain about having an allergy. Somebody might complain about needing to have a bandage upon some minor wound; right?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes. This is what we usually did on -- but I think that on the basis of the diagnosis one knows what the treatment is or should be. I said that I wasn't the one who kept the notes, so I don't think I am in a position to give you more details.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, with regard to somebody who had -- had a chronic condition, one of the things that you wanted to make sure of, whether you kept the notes or not, Doctor, was that there was a record of your contact with that particular patient so that you could chart what was going on; right?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: We worked in extraordinary conditions, so it wasn't possible for us to keep very exact or regular notes with all the details. We did what we could under the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand. With regard to the injections that were administered which you discussed with Mr. Whiting but ago -- a moment ago --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could I please have the usher give the good doctor P217.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You have a list here that begins on the 31st of May and continues up to and including the 25th of July; correct? Perhaps it's the 24th, the last entry.

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It contains -- it contains the name -- the names of some 84 individuals or 84 incidents in which injections were administered, and from what I understand your testimony to be, we can feel comfortable that that is an accurate list of the injections that were administered during your tenure at the Lapusnik clinic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to object to the characterisation of the testimony. I think the witness has been very clear that they did the best they could on the records.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The matter was put as a question. I think the witness is well able to decide whether the question affects his understanding or not. Carry on, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you have my question in mind, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Can you please repeat it? I'm not clear about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Surely. That list contains the name of some 84 individuals or 84 incidents in which injections were administered; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes, it must be so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And from what I understand your testimony to be, we can feel comfortable that this is an accurate list of the injections that were administered during your tenure at the Lapusnik clinic; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes, but as I said earlier, I'm not certain as to the origin of the list - I mean, on the -- whether the list was drawn on the basis of the names, the last names whom I think are from Lapusnik and the surrounding villages - which shows that the services have been administered in that clinic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I have -- I have one brief question, and perhaps you can be of some help. With regard to the very last injection that was administered, if you look at that list, could you tell us what the date was of that?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I think it must be 24th of July, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, apart from giving people injections at your clinic, among -- you also, as we have discussed, gave them medication; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, in going through the records that have been shown to you by Mr. Whiting, I have not come across the name of Haradin Bala as being a patient of yours or having any contact in the clinic in any of the documents that have thus far been presented to you, and if you would just take my word for that for the moment. One of the things that I'm trying to understand here is you've told us that you saw Haradin Bala on one or two occasions; right?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You've indicated that you believe that you saw him sometime between the period of the beginning of June to sometime in the end of July; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I think so, even though I'm unable to give you an exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We previously discussed that when you spoke to the investigator, Mr. Tucker, you had indicated the month of May as being the starting point for your work at Lapusnik, which you said, if I'm not mistaken, may have been a mistake when you said May back in 2003; right?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I said maybe he has wrongly put the time, the person who did the interview. I -- this I didn't see, I think, at that time when he must have written it down.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. When you say that -- that you didn't see it when he wrote it down, are you saying that you never said to Mr. Tucker the month of May? You never indicated to Mr. Tucker that your clinic commenced in the month of May? Is that what your testimony is, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I may tell you that it started at the end of May and the beginning of June. Just a matter of one day. And my testimony is that we began work there in the beginning of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So you're clear, Mr. Bala maintains that he came to Lapusnik shortly after the first battle in May. And when do you believe that first battle was? Because I believe that you said you were in Lapusnik at that time.

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: The first battle, I think, must have been sometime on the 8th of May, the first clash between the KLA and the Serb occupiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In the village of Lapusnik, do you know whether or not any of Haradin Bala's relatives live there?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And who would that be?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: The Thaqi family.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Is that -- is that Ali Thaqi?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Bala maintains that he left Lapusnik by the end of May, certainly the very beginning of June, and it must have been that period of time that you saw him.

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I don't remember the accurate date. I'm telling you I commenced in the beginning of June. It was either the 1st or the 2nd of June, I'm not sure. This is when I started work.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, when Mr. Bala came to see you for his check-up, he told you that he was complaining of, as I think you said, arrythmia. True?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: To my recollection, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And as I understand your testimony, you indicated that he had some medication with him which were in the form of beta blockers. He may have had some other medication. And you checked his blood pressure. Right?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, do you -- as you sit here today, do you have any -- any memory of making any records of what his blood pressure was at that time and whether or not he was in any, shall we say, crisis?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I don't remember something like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When an individual complains of arrythmia, as a doctor, what does that indicate?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: It indicates that he's suffering from a serious condition, that his cardiovascular system has problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, perhaps you can be of some help to us here. Is one of the things that can affect the cardiovascular system temperature, and by that I mean the ambient temperature?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: It may affect it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you recall what the temperature was in the months of -- roughly in the month of May of 1998? And I know that covers a great period of time. I'm not asking you to give me each day the temperature, but was it a hot summer?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I don't remember. I know that May usually in our country is not very hot.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: How about June?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: June is usually hot.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the long hot summer of 1998, is that an accurate statement that it was a hot summer and the months of June and July were unseasonably warm?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I didn't notice, as far as I remember, them to be unseasonably warm.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: An individual who has a serious cardiovascular condition who is in an area such as Lapusnik during the summer months, is that an individual who is going to be able to engage in heavy physical exertion? Can you tell us, Doctor, if you know from your medical expertise?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I don't think he can engage in strenuous physical activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you think that an individual who suffers from such a condition would be able to, for example, chop a tree for ten or 15 minutes?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: No, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: How about take a stick and beat somebody for half an hour continuously?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I don't know what answer to give you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, from the standpoint of the kind of exertion that would take, and perhaps you can once again be of some help to us because of your expertise in this regard, I take it that when somebody engages in -- in some form of physical exertion a variety of things happen physiologically to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to object, Your Honour. First of all, I think these questions are extremely vague and speculative. Secondly, the witness has not testified that he has any expertise in this area, that is with heart trouble, cardiovascular trouble. In fact, he specifically said his speciality is general medicine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think that the objection as put is not one of critical significance, Mr. Guy-Smith, except for the introductory comment that -- the vagueness and speculation. I don't perceive where you're heading or why, but I've about quiet on the assumption that you've got good reason, but the way it's being put would make it very hard on the limited experience and knowledge of the present witness and his recollection back to that time of what is apparently a very limited recollection of having seen your client to try and give very general answers to extremely general questions as to what might or might not be physically possible or what might be the effects of doing things. It seems extremely tenuous.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I appreciate the -- well, to say that I appreciate is not exactly correct, but I understand the Court's thinking, and I think that the Court understands the dilemma that I have. Unfortunately, there wasn't a cardiovascular specialist in Kosovo at the time who was able to engage in a comprehensive work-up of Mr. Bala at that point in time, so I'm working with the -- in the same way that the good doctor was working at the time with limited resources, I'm working at the time with the limited resources that we have. But understanding what you have just said, I won't pursue it much further, because I don't think that it's going to be given much attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, how can you assume that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I don't know why. It just seems that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You've told us that you were born in Lapusnik, and I take it you know the area well, do you not, Doctor? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I know the area well, and I know the area which is down in the valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. When you say "down in the valley," if I understood your testimony correctly, you also told us that on, I believe it was the 25th - I may be mistaken - you fled and went into the Berisha mountains; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the distance from Lapusnik up into the Berisha mountains, I believe, to the first village you went to was some number of kilometres. True?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And could you tell us about how far that was?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I cannot give you an exact estimate, but maybe four or five kilometres from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, since you've indicated a valley and you've also indicated a mountain, there's obviously some kind of a height difference between the two. There's not only a distance that one travels in terms of length but in terms of height. Could you tell us, if you know, approximately how high up the mountain you go? How many feet up did you go from the valley up to -- up to the Berisha mountains?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: You mean the height above the sea level?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, you know what, if you were in a position to tell us what the height was of the valley and the height above the sea level that mountains were, that would be fine, if you can do that.

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: The distance, as I said, between Lapusnik and Berisha is about four or five kilometres, but I have no information as to the altitude or height. Probably -- certainly it is higher. It is obviously higher.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: For you, when you took that walk in July, when you were fleeing, was that an easy walk for you to make up that mountain?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: It was not at all an easy walk.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Why is that?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Because we were under constant volley of bullets fired by the enemy while we were climbing the mountain track. The trek was full of obstacles, stones. A mountain path, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you think your heart rate went up as you were climbing up that mountain?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, you've told Mr. Whiting that you never went into any prison camp at Lapusnik; right?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes, this is what I've told him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's the truth; right?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes, that's the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You never heard of a prison camp in Lapusnik; correct? I don't know if they heard your answer.

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And that's the truth; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes, that's the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And you've told Mr. Whiting that you knew of a fellow by the name of -- a name that I'm not supposed to mention in public session. If you recall it, I will -- let's just go into private session for a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And that gentleman said that he went with you to a prison camp where you saw an Albanian boy who had been beaten and said that you couldn't help him. Is that true? Did you do that?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: It is not true. I have never visited anyone in any prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Can you think of any reason why that gentleman or that individual would say such a thing?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I cannot. I don't know why he said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: This seems to be a question that I ask a fair number of people, and I'll ask this question of you, too, sir: How tall are you?
