utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Around 1.93 or 94 centimetres -- metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think you would consider yourself to be a tall man, would you not?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: This is how others call me as well. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And in describing Haradin Bala, you said that he was a man, I think using your words, of average height; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I said that Haradin Bala was rather tall. I don't know how this was translated or interpreted. He isn't of average height, but he is rather tall.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could you tell us when you use the term "average height" what you mean? What do you consider to be average height?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: What I thought was that he wasn't of an average height, he was between the average and the maximum height.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Once again, what do you consider to be an average height, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I don't know how this was interpreted to you. I really don't know how to explain this, because you have short, average, and tall. There are persons who fall between the average and maximum height. This is what I thought when I described him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you this question, then, and perhaps I can be a bit more specific for you and you can be of assistance: A person who was, let's say, 1.76 metres, would that person be short, average, tall, or where would they fit into your definition of height?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: A little bit beyond the average height.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: A little bit beyond the average. Certainly not tall, then, right?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you spoke to Mr. Tucker back in 2003, you told him, among other things, if I'm not mistaken - and I'm trying to find the exact place here for you - that as far as you knew, you were the only doctor working -- working in that particular area; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you were defining that area, what specific area were you referring to then? Was that just the Lapusnik area proper, right around Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: The area of Lapusnik and some other villages falling in that area. We had cases when patients from other villages visited us in our clinic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you recall what other clinics were in the general area of Lapusnik apart from the one place that you've mentioned, which I believe was a more established clinic in Malisevo?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I think that there was an outpatient clinic in Orlat village, but to my knowledge they didn't have medical personnel there. There was another outpatient clinic in Negrovc village, which is a little bit further away.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: What about the village of Shale?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Which village do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The village proper of Shale.

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: The village of Shale, the village with the name of Shale, Sedlare?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Shale village was about seven to ten kilometres in the southern part of Lapusnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And that would be, in your estimation, a considerable distance away, would it not?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith. Mr. Powles.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Doctor Gashi, my name is Steven Powles, and I represent Isak Musliu, who I think you know, who sits behind me. You stated in your evidence that you were able to study at Pristina University, but there came a time in Kosovo where Kosovo Albanians were forced to leave the official university system; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: You were forced to study in a parallel system. Similarly, is it correct that during that time Kosovo Albanians were forced to leave certain forms of employment to make way for Serb employees? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: And it's right, isn't it, that you were not able to practice as a -- as an official doctor in Kosovo during the early 1990s following your qualification.

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Would you agree with me in saying, therefore, that at that time Kosovo Albanians were really treated as second-class citizens in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Moving on to May, June, and July of 1998, when you were in Lapusnik, you stated in your evidence that the Serbs and Yugoslav forces were shelling Lapusnik from Komorane; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Now, it may be that you can't help with this, but it may be that you can. In your opinion, if they had wanted to, were the Yugoslav forces able to target and destroy a particular building from Komorane had they wanted to?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to object to lack of foundation for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It seems a big ask of a medically trained person, Mr. Powles. I think the question is just too far off beat.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Maybe I can try it another way.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: While you were in Lapusnik, Doctor, was it your impression that civilians who were in Lapusnik and civilian property in Lapusnik was at risk from Serb shelling?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: In your capacity as a medical expert in Lapusnik at that time, did you have to deal with any civilians who had suffered injuries as a result of such shelling?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: We didn't have cases that resulted of shelling. This is now my opinion, because I'm not an expert in logistics, but there were no casualties because of the geographical position that Lapusnik had. Many of persons that I knew removed their families from there to other villages which were safer.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Doctor, it's right that you were not actually in the KLA, were you?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: And no pressure was placed upon you at any time to join the KLA, was it?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: No, there wasn't any.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: And the medical assistance that you gave in Lapusnik in the summer of 1998, that was assistance that you gave voluntarily, wasn't it, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Now, you were in charge of the medical assistance being given in Lapusnik at that time. Is it right, Doctor, that there were two other people dealing with other matters of a non-military nature in Lapusnik at that time; a Mr. Ymer Sopi was assisting with logistics and a Mr. Rasim Gashi was assisting with physical labour and building positions. Is that something that you knew at that time, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I have no idea about that because I exclusively dealt with providing medical assistance to those who needed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: It's right, isn't it, Doctor, that during your time in Lapusnik you saw no members of the military police operating at that time, May, June, and July of 1998?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. What military police do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: It's right, isn't it, Doctor, that you did not see any KLA soldiers wearing black uniforms with the military police PU emblem on their arms?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: Soldiers with black uniforms, to my recollection, I have seen such soldiers, but as I explained, I exclusively dealt with medical issues, and we paid no interest as of other matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: But those soldiers wearing black uniforms, it's right that they were not members of the military police, or is that something that you don't know, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: ZEQIR GASHI
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see the time. I've got a little bit more for the doctor but not much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I am afraid we must finish now, and you'll have to take up the running again tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: I'm very grateful, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Dr. Gashi, we have to finish now, and we resume tomorrow at 2.15. If you could return to finish your evidence then. Thank you. We are adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 12th day of April, 2005, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.01 p.m.,
